shell.signOutTitle: Ends this portal session and the sign-on session behind it — this browser's sessions. It does not revoke tokens or tickets already issued to applications; Sign out of everything, on the Overview page, does.
shell.refreshTitle: Draws this page again with what this service holds now.
rules.development: This service is in development mode and checks no password, so any password is accepted here. In product mode it must be {rules}.
activate.title: Set up your account
activate.sub: You are setting up how {name} will sign in to {base}.
activate.eitherNote: Leave both empty if you would rather sign in with a passkey alone. You need at least one of the two.
activate.passkeyNote: A passkey — on this device, your phone or a security key — can be used INSTEAD of a password or as a SECOND step after it.
activate.rolePrimary: Use a passkey instead of a password
activate.roleMfa: Use a passkey as a second step, after the password above
activate.passkeyStepNote: Choosing a passkey takes you to one more screen after this step, and your account is not set up until the passkey is created.
activate.totpBox: Also set up an authenticator app as a second factor
activate.totpNote: A six-digit code from Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, Authy, 1Password, Bitwarden, Aegis, FreeOTP or any other app that implements RFC 6238. It is a SECOND factor — it works beside the password or passkey above and never instead of one. Ticking this shows you a QR code on the next step; your account is not set up until you type a code back from it.
activateTotp.title: Set up your authenticator app
activateTotp.sub: Almost done. {name} can sign in now; this adds the second factor.
activateTotp.note: Nothing about the authenticator is stored until this code checks out, and your activation link is not used up until then either — so if you cannot finish now, open the link again and leave the authenticator box unticked.
totp.scanHeading: Scan this with your authenticator app
totp.qrAlt: QR code carrying this account's otpauth setup URI
totp.codeLabel: The {digits}-digit code your app is showing now
activateKey.subPrimary: Almost done. {name} will sign in with this passkey and no password.
activateKey.subMfa: Almost done. {name} will sign in with this passkey as a second step, after the password.
activateKey.notUntil: Your account is not set up, and this activation link is not used up, until the passkey is created.
activateKey.cannot: If you cannot create a passkey now, open your activation link again and choose differently.
key.promptSecurityKey: Your browser is about to ask for your security key. Insert or tap it when it asks.
key.promptPasskey: Your browser is about to ask where to save your passkey — this device (Touch ID, Face ID, Windows Hello or the screen lock), your password manager, or your phone.
key.didNotAsk: My browser did not ask — tell me why
ready.title: Account ready
ready.heading: Your account is ready
ready.okPassword: Your password is set. This activation link has now been used and will not work again.
ready.okSetUp: Your account is set up. This activation link has now been used and will not work again.
ready.totp: Your authenticator app is set up. You will be asked for a code every time you sign in, after your password — a password alone will not get you in any more. The code you just typed is spent, so wait for the next one.
ready.keyPrimary: Your passkey is ready and is how you sign in. At the sign-in screen, type your username, tick Sign in with a passkey instead of a password and leave the password empty. Create a second passkey on your Passkeys page once you are in, so that losing this one is not a locked account.
ready.keyMfa: Your passkey is ready as a second step. You will be asked for it every time you sign in, after your password.
reset.title: Choose a new password
reset.sub: You are choosing the password {name} signs in to {base} with. Once it is set, no password you had before works.
directory.name: Name
directory.fromSession: from your session rather than from a directory entry
directory.notShowing: This service is not showing your directory entry. Either it is running without its embedded directory, or nothing has been written down about you yet — an account here gets an entry the first time it authenticates or is provisioned. What is above is what the sign-in itself carried.
directory.secret: — a scrypt hash rather than the value, and never shown here
directory.binaryMany: — {bytes} bytes of binary in {count} values, not shown
directory.requiredTitle: The schema REQUIRES this attribute on every person.
directory.nothingFromClass: Nothing on your entry from this class.
directory.heading: Your directory entry
directory.every: Every attribute the schema this service files people under allows — {held} of {total} are set on your entry. It is a fixed list read from the schema rather than a dump of what your entry happens to carry, so a credential this service stores beside these cannot appear here.
directory.notEditable: Nothing on this page can be edited here. These are written by an operator, by SCIM, or over LDAP — this portal changes how you AUTHENTICATE and not what this directory records about you.
overview.youSub: What this identity provider knows about you, and how you signed in to this page.
overview.subject: Subject
overview.authentications: ({n, plural, one {# authentication} other {# authentications}} in this sign-in)
overview.requiredPasskeyOrCode: required — a password alone will not sign you in. You will be asked for your passkey, with a one-time code offered as the alternative.
overview.requiredPasskey: required — a password alone will not sign you in. You will be asked for your passkey.
overview.requiredCode: required — a password alone will not sign you in. You will be asked for a code from your authenticator app.
overview.signOutAllNote: Ends every session you hold here, in every protocol, and tells the applications that can be told — access and refresh tokens, Kerberos tickets, credential offers, LDAP binds, the lot. The Sign out button at the top of every page is the narrower one: it ends this browser's sessions and leaves what has already been issued to applications alone. Two different acts, and this is the one that reaches further.
language.heading: Language and region
language.current: Your account's language is {name}. Pages here, and the sign-in screens, are drawn in it wherever a translation exists.
language.none: Your account names no language, so pages follow the language your browser asks for, or the one you last chose at the top of a page.
language.label: Language
language.note: This is the preferredLanguage on your own directory entry. An application that asks for a particular language when it sends you to sign in still gets it.
password.none: You have NO password set. Setting one here needs the current one, which you do not have — so a password is set through an activation link from whoever administers this service, or at /portal/activate.
password.note: Your current password is required even though you are already signed in: a session somebody left open on a shared machine must not be enough to take the account over.
attest.unanchored: verified, from an authenticator no trusted root vouches for
keys.nicknameSecurityKey: Give your security key a nickname so you know which one this is when you see it here later.
keys.nicknamePasskey: Give your passkey a nickname so you know which one this is when you see it here later.
keys.intro: Passkeys can be created and saved on your devices, like your phone or laptop, or on security keys. A passkey is an encrypted digital key you unlock with your fingerprint, face or screen lock; most are saved to your password manager, so you can sign in on your other devices too. On a security key, the key stays on that one small device.
keys.someSecond: At least one of these is a second step after your password, so a password alone will not sign you in.
keys.noneSecond: None of these is a second step after your password.
keys.lastWayIn: You cannot remove your last way in — set another one first.
keys.noneYet: You have no passkeys yet. Create one below, on this device or your phone, or use a security key.
keys.canBackUp: can be backed up, not yet
keys.syncedRefused: This passkey can be synced, and this realm now accepts only device-bound passkeys, so it will not sign you in. Remove it and register a security key or a passkey kept on one device.
keys.usedMfa: as a second step after your password (mfa)
keys.learnRoles: A passkey here is either instead of your password — it signs you in on its own — or a second step after your password. You choose which when you create it.
keys.learnWhere: A passkey on your devices is usually saved to a password manager (iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password and others), so it is there on your other devices too. A passkey on a security key stays on that key, and a certified security key is the strongest kind of sign-in there is.
keys.learnDevicesBefore: To link a phone or computer on
keys.learnDevicesAfter: , create the passkey on that device; a passkey on a security key identifies no device.
keys.learnMany: You hold {n}, which is the point. If one is lost, the others still sign you in — and you can remove the lost one here without asking anybody.
keys.learnOne: You hold one and no backup. If it is lost, an operator has to clear it for you before you can create another — there is deliberately no self-service reset of a credential you cannot produce. Create a second one now, on a different device or a security key.
keys.learnNoPassword: You have no password. A passkey used as a second step needs one.
kind.passkey: A passkey on this device or your phone
kind.passkeyWhat: Touch ID, Face ID, Windows Hello, the screen lock or your password manager. Most passkeys are there on your other devices too.
kind.securityKeyWhat: A USB, NFC or Bluetooth key you carry. The passkey stays on the key.
enrol.heading: Add a passkey
enrol.off: Passkeys are switched off in this service, so no new one can be created. Any passkey already on your account goes on working.
enrol.atCap: You hold {n} passkeys, which is the most this service allows. Remove one first.
enrol.different: Use a DIFFERENT one from any already on your account — the point of a backup is that it is not in the same place as the original. One that is already registered will refuse.
enrol.creatingKeyPrimary: Creating: a passkey on a security key, used instead of your password.
enrol.creatingKeyMfa: Creating: a passkey on a security key, used as a second step after your password.
enrol.creatingDevicePrimary: Creating: a passkey on your device, used instead of your password.
enrol.creatingDeviceMfa: Creating: a passkey on your device, used as a second step after your password.
enrol.asSecond: As a second step after my password
enrol.asSecondWhat: You will be asked for it every time you sign in.
enrol.asSecondNoPassword: You have no password, so this passkey alone will not sign you in — set a password as well.
enrol.insteadWhat: You sign in with the passkey and nothing else.
enrol.noRole: This service allows a passkey in neither role at the moment, so none can be created.
enrol.addsNew: This adds a NEW passkey. The ones you already hold are excluded, so choosing one that is already registered will refuse rather than adding it twice.
emailFactor.heading: Email as a second factor
emailFactor.noMail: This service cannot send mail just now.
emailFactor.unverified: Your address is not verified. Verify it on the Email page first.
emailFactor.onCode: On: after your password, a six-digit code is sent to {address}.
emailFactor.onLink: On: after your password, a sign-in link is sent to {address}.
emailFactor.unusedCode: You chose an emailed code, but it is not being used: {why}.
emailFactor.unusedLink: You chose an emailed link, but it is not being used: {why}.
emailFactor.weakest: Email is the weakest second factor this service offers. Anybody who can read your mailbox — with your email password alone, often — can finish signing in as you, which is why NIST SP 800-63B-4 does not count email as an authenticator. An authenticator app or a passkey is better where you have one; you are asked for those first.
mfa.setUp: An authenticator app is set up. A password alone will not sign you in — you will be asked for a code.
mfa.unreadable: An authenticator app is enrolled, but this service cannot read the enrolment, so it cannot check your codes. An administrator has to clear it before you can set one up again.
mfa.none: No authenticator app is set up.
mfa.doors: While you use a second factor, your password alone is refused at the doors that cannot ask for one ({doors}).
mfa.makeAppPasswordAfter: for a client that uses one of them.
mfa.removeNote: Removing it drops your account to one factor. It cannot lock you out — an authenticator app is never a way in by itself — but your password alone will sign you in again afterwards.
mfa.notSavedYet: Nothing is saved until you type a code back, so this is not set up yet.
mfa.byHand: If you cannot scan — the phone is showing this page, the app has no camera, or this service is on localhost and your phone cannot reach it — add the account by hand with these:
mfa.spent: The code this service accepts here is SPENT — you will need the next one to sign in, which is RFC 6238 section 5.2 and is why a code never works twice.
mfa.anyApp: Use your favourite authenticator app — Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, Authy, 1Password, Bitwarden, Aegis, FreeOTP, KeePassXC or any other. They all implement the same specification (RFC 6238), so any of them works and nothing here is tied to one.
mfa.replaces: Setting up a new one replaces the one you have. You hold one authenticator here and not a list, because a six-digit code says nothing about which app produced it. Delete the old account from your app afterwards — it will keep showing codes that no longer work.
mfa.startAgain: Start again with a new secret
mfa.turnedOff: Authenticator apps are turned off on this service. An operator turns them on in the authentication policy.
mfa.about: A time-based one-time password — RFC 6238. Your app and this service hold the same secret and both compute the same {digits}-digit number from it and the clock, so the code proves you have the app without either of you sending the secret anywhere. It changes every {period} seconds.
mfa.aboutSecond: It is a SECOND factor and never a first one. It cannot replace your password here, because this service holds the same secret your app does — which is fine for proving you still have the app, and is not something to hang a whole account on. That is the difference between this and a security key, which keeps a private key this service never sees.
mfa.aboutChecked: Codes are checked properly, in every mode. Most credentials on this mock are not — any password is accepted — but a one-time password verifier that accepted any six digits would not be a permissive one, it would be a broken one, and there would be nothing left to test a client against.
codes.notSavedYet: They are not saved yet. Nothing has been stored, and none of these codes will work until you press the button below.
codes.plainText: The same codes as plain text, one per line
codes.onlyTime: This is the only time they will ever be shown. When you confirm, this service stores a hash of each one — the same kind of scrypt hash it stores for your password — so it can check a code you type and can never print one back. Write them down, print them, or put them in a password manager first.
codes.eachOnce: Each code works once. Type one at the sign-in screen instead of your second factor when you cannot produce it. The dashes and the case do not matter; they are there so you can transcribe it.
codes.confirmReplaces: Confirming replaces the set you already have. Every code on your old list stops working the moment you press the button.
codes.closeWithout: If you close this page without confirming, nothing is stored and nothing changes — these codes simply never existed. Whatever set you had before is untouched.
codes.advised: You have a second factor and no recovery codes. If you cannot reach it — a flat phone, a security key in a drawer at home — there is currently no way back into this account except an administrator.
codes.noneGenerated: None have been generated. Recovery codes stand in for a second factor when you cannot produce it, so they are worth generating once you have one.
codes.willNotCreate: This service will not create a set for you. It used to, as a side effect of enrolling a second factor — it cannot any more, because it now stores only a hash of each code and a hash can only be made while the code is on the screen in front of you.
codes.howMany: {count} codes of {length} characters are generated. They are shown once, and stored only after you confirm you have saved them.
codes.unreadable: A set exists and this service cannot read it ({why}), so a code you type cannot be checked against it.
codes.unreadableFix: Generating a new set replaces it and fixes this. An administrator can also clear it from your row under /admin/users.
codes.unusedOf: {remaining} of your {total} recovery codes are unused.
codes.storedHow: as a scrypt hash of each code — the same way your password is stored, which is why they cannot be shown to you again
codes.noWayToSee: There is no way to see these again. Generating a new set shows you ten new codes and replaces the ones you have — every code on your current list stops working. Only do it if you have lost them or have used most of them.
codes.allUsed: Every code has been used. There is nothing left to fall back on until you generate a new set.
codes.nearlyOut: You are nearly out. {remaining} left of {total}. They are not topped up.
codes.heading: Recovery codes
codes.turnedOff: Recovery codes are turned off on this realm's authentication policy, so no new set can be generated. A set already saved goes on working — a setting that took away the only way back into an account whose phone is lost would be the worst switch here.
signingKey.samlHow: What to do with it. Build a SAML 2.0 <Assertion> whose <Issuer> and <Subject><NameID> are both {who}, with an <Audience> and a bearer <SubjectConfirmationData Recipient> of {endpoint} and a NotOnOrAfter a minute or two ahead. Sign it with an enveloped XML Signature using this key, base64url-encode the document, and present it to the token endpoint as an RFC 7522 section 2.1 authorization grant. This service matches the signature to the certificate it holds for you, thumbprint {thumbprint}.
signingKey.samlOnlyYou: The <Subject> can only ever be you. An assertion signed with this key that names somebody else is refused — the key says who you are, and it is not permission to speak for anybody.
signingKey.jwtHow: What to do with it. Sign a JSON Web Token with it and present that to the token endpoint as an RFC 7523 section 2.1 authorization grant. The claims are iss and sub both {who}, an aud of {endpoint}, an exp a minute or two ahead, and a jti you do not reuse. The header carries alg {alg} and kid {kid}.
signingKey.jwtOnlyYou: `sub` can only ever be you. An assertion signed with this key that names somebody else is refused — the key says who you are, and it is not permission to speak for anybody.
signingKey.certificate: Your certificate (public — this is the half anybody may hold)
signingKey.replaces: Generating replaces what you have. The {rfc} key you hold now stops being accepted the moment the new one is written, and anything signing with it starts being refused. Your other signing key, if you hold one, is untouched.
signingKey.shownOnce: The private half is shown once, on the page that comes back. Nothing here can show it to you again.
signingKey.notRevocation: This is not revocation. The certificate stays valid and still chains to this service’s root; what changes is that this service stops accepting what the key signs, because the key is no longer registered against you. Your other signing key, your password, your passkeys and your authenticator app are untouched — this is not a way you sign in.
tls.heading: TLS client certificate
tls.what: A TLS client certificate signs you in with no password typed: your browser presents it when a server asks, and this identity provider recognises it as you. It is issued from this realm’s TLS client certificate authority, names you (CN={name} and urn:sts:person:{name}), and carries clientAuth. You download it once, as a password-protected .p12, and install it in each browser or device you want to sign in from.
tls.whereWorksAfter: . This service asks every connection for a client certificate and requires none, so your browser sends this one when you choose it; that page starts a sign-on session for you in this realm, and your other applications here then sign you in without asking. Your browser will first ask you to trust this service’s server certificate if it does not already.
tls.notAccepted: This service will not accept it at the moment.
tls.name: Name
tls.compromised: Somebody else may have the key
tls.noneHeld: You have no TLS client certificate.
tls.atCap: You hold {n} valid TLS client certificates, which is the most this service issues to one person. Revoke one you no longer use to make room.
tls.labelName: Name it after the browser or device (optional)
tls.p12Password: A password for the downloaded file
tls.p12Note: This password protects the private key inside the file while it sits on your disk; your browser asks for it once, when you import the file. It is not your account password, and this service does not keep it.
tls.generate: Generate and download my TLS client certificate
tls.revokingIs: Revoking is revocation. The certificate goes on this realm’s certificate revocation list, its OCSP responder answers revoked, and the TLS listeners refuse it from then on. It cannot be undone; generate a new one instead.
tlsFresh.heading: Save your TLS client certificate
tlsFresh.onlyTime: This is the only time these files can be downloaded. The private key is not kept by this service — not on this page, not by an administrator. If you lose the files, revoke this certificate below and generate a new one.
tlsFresh.files: The .p12 holds the private key, your certificate and the two certificate authorities above it, protected by the password you just chose. The -key.pem is the same key encrypted under the same password, and -chain.pem is the certificates alone — both for command-line tools.
tlsFresh.win1: Open the downloaded {file}. The Certificate Import Wizard starts.
tlsFresh.win2: Choose Current User, keep the file, and type the file password.
tlsFresh.win3: Let Windows choose the store automatically, and finish.
tlsFresh.macTitle: Chrome, Edge or Safari on macOS
tlsFresh.mac1: Open the downloaded {file}. Keychain Access offers to add it to the login keychain.
tlsFresh.mac3: Chrome, Edge and Safari all use that keychain.
tlsFresh.firefox1: Open Settings → Privacy & Security and scroll to Certificates.
tlsFresh.firefox2: Press View Certificates…, open the Your Certificates tab and press Import….
tlsFresh.firefox3: Choose {file} and type the file password.
tlsFresh.linux2: Press Import, choose {file} and type the file password.
tlsFresh.legacy: If a macOS release older than your browser refuses the .p12 with a message about the password, rebuild it with the older algorithms it expects: openssl pkcs12 -export -legacy -inkey {key} -in {chain} -out legacy.p12.
tlsFresh.useChoose: in the browser you installed it in and choose this certificate when asked. What comes back says whether it signed you in and who as; then come back to
tlsFresh.useAfter: , which will not ask you to sign in again.
signingKey.onlyTime: This is the only time it will be shown. It is stored on your entry encrypted, and nothing in this service — not this page, not an administrator — can print it again. Copy it now; if you lose it, generate a new key pair, which replaces this one.
signingKey.what: A signing key lets something act as you without a browser: a script or a service signs a short-lived document with it and this identity provider hands back an access token for you. No password is typed and no sign-in screen is drawn — the signature is the whole of it.
signingKey.twoKinds: There are two kinds, one per document format, and they are separate key pairs: RFC 7523’s JWT bearer authorization grant signs a JSON Web Token, and RFC 7522’s SAML 2.0 bearer authorization grant signs a SAML assertion. A key issued for one is refused by the other. This service issues each key pair from its own certificate authority, keeps the public half on your entry to check signatures with, and gives you the private half once.
signingKey.thirdCard: The third card is a different kind of key: a
signingKey.thirdCardAfter: , which signs you in from a browser rather than letting a script act as you.
signingKey.noEntry: This service holds no entry for you, so there is nowhere to put a key pair.
signingKey.noAuthority: Nothing can be issued here at the moment. This service has no certificate authority in this realm, and building one is an administrator’s job rather than something this page can do.
signingKey.notOffered: This service does not let people issue their own signing keys (pki.personSelfService is off). An administrator can still issue one to you.
signingKey.unaffected: The keys you already hold are unaffected and go on working.
apps.unlinkedTitle: This application has not told this identity provider where it lives, so there is nothing to link to. Whoever administers this service can set its home page on the application's entry.
apps.withheld: not {families} — the policy permits the {n, plural, one {other} other {others}}
apps.nothing: There is nothing here yet. Either this service has no applications registered that sign people in, or the issuance policy does not permit you any of them.
apps.sub: Where this identity provider will sign you in. Each row was decided by the SAME policy the token endpoint, both SAML profiles and WS-Federation ask before they issue anything — so this page and those endpoints cannot disagree.
apps.notListed: What is not on this list
apps.notPermittedWhat: {n} {n, plural, one {application} other {applications}}. They are counted rather than named: which applications exist here is not a question this page answers. Whoever administers this service decides, by giving your account a role the application requires.
apps.notDestinationsWhat: {n} {n, plural, one {entry} other {entries}}. A registered application is not necessarily somewhere a person signs in — a Shared Signals receiver, a SCIM provisioning client, an LDAP binder, a SPIFFE workload or a WS-Trust relying party is an application this service knows and not a door you walk through.
apps.notLookedWhat: {skipped} of {total} entries. This page evaluates the issuance policy for each application it lists and stops at {limit} (portal.applicationScanLimit), because that work happens on the one thread answering every socket this service holds.
apps.note: A name in blue links to the application's own home page and hands it nothing — it is where you would go yourself, and a sign-in starts there. A name in grey means this identity provider has not been told where that application lives; whoever administers this service can set a home page on its entry, and until then there is nothing to link to. Sign in appears only beside an OpenID Connect application that registered an initiate_login_uri: it asks that application to start a sign-in here, naming this identity provider and you (OpenID Connect Core section 4). Nothing else starts a sign-in for you: this service implements no identity-provider-initiated sign-on in the browser profiles — /saml2 says so on its own page — so such a link would have to invent a request the application never asked for.
risc.heading: Sharing security events about your account
risc.alwaysShared: Security events about this account are shared, and cannot be stopped from here.
risc.shared: Security events about your account are shared with the applications that receive them.
risc.stoppingSince: You asked to stop sharing security events on {since} and it takes effect {hours} hour(s) after you asked. Until then they are still shared, and you can cancel.
risc.stopping: You asked to stop sharing security events and it takes effect {hours} hour(s) after you asked. Until then they are still shared, and you can cancel.
risc.notShared: Security events about your account are not shared, apart from the notice that you opted out.
risc.note: These are OpenID RISC events: an account disabled, a password that must be changed, a contact detail changed. Applications you use receive them to protect your account there. Stopping them is your choice (RISC section 2.8), and it waits {hours} hour(s) so that somebody who has taken your account over cannot silence them at once.
signals.incomplete: This portal is not currently being told about everything that happens to your account, so this list may be incomplete. An administrator can see why on
signals.consoleCopy: the console's copy of this page
signals.verified: signed by this identity provider and verified
signals.couldNot: this portal could not sign you out here
signals.left: this portal left you signed in here ({why})
signals.would: this portal would sign you out here (development mode records it only)
signals.signedOut: this portal signed you out here
signals.noSession: this portal had no session of yours to end
signals.empty: Nothing has been reported about your account yet. This list fills when this identity provider tells this portal that something happened to one of your sessions or to your account — a sign-in, a sign-out, a session revoked, an account disabled or enabled, an identifier changed.
signals.heading: What has been reported about your account
signals.sub: This portal is a registered receiver of this identity provider's security event feed. When something happens to one of your sessions or to your account, a signed notice is delivered here — and this is every one of them that was about you.
signals.isNot: What this list is, and what it is not
signals.onlyYou: Only the notices about you are here. This portal is told about everybody it serves, and what you are shown is narrowed to the notices whose subject is you. Where a notice names somebody in a way this service cannot match to an account — a phone number, for instance — it is left out rather than guessed at, so it is possible for something about you to be missing from this list. It is never possible for something about somebody else to be on it.
signals.record: This list is a record and not a control (the one control on this page is whether events are shared at all, above). Nothing in it can be edited or removed, including by you: a list of what was said about your account would be worth nothing if the account's owner could empty it.
signals.toChange: ; to change a credential, use the pages in How you sign in.
signals.caepRisc: The notices are OpenID CAEP (what happened to a session) and OpenID RISC (what happened to an account) events, carried over the Shared Signals Framework and signed by this identity provider. Each one was verified against its signature before it was recorded here; a notice that did not verify is shown saying so rather than hidden.
resetDone.title: Password set
resetDone.heading: Your password is set
resetDone.ok: This reset link has now been used and will not work again.
resetDone.next: Sign in with your new password. If your account has a second factor, you will be asked for it as usual.
signedOut.title: Signed out
signedOut.heading: You are signed out
signedOut.noSession: There was no portal session on this browser to end.
signedOut.endedAll: Your portal session has ended, and so has the admin console session it was made from, and so has the sign-on session it was built on — so anything else you were signed in to through it is signed out too.
signedOut.endedConsole: Your portal session has ended, and so has the admin console session it was made from. There was no sign-on session left behind it to end.
signedOut.endedSignOn: Your portal session has ended, and so has the sign-on session it was built on — so anything else you were signed in to through it is signed out too.
signedOut.endedPortal: Your portal session has ended. There was no sign-on session left behind it to end.
signedOut.why: Signing out of the portal alone would not have signed you out: this portal is an ordinary OpenID Connect client of this service (sts-user-portal), so the next page would have run the sign-in flow again, met the sign-on session and let you back in with nothing to type.
signedOut.tokens: Tokens, tickets and other credentials already issued to applications are untouched.
signedOut.logoutLists: lists all of them and ends what you choose.
done.emailOn: Email is now your second factor, after your password.
done.emailOff: Email is no longer a second factor for you.
done.totpSetUp: Your authenticator app is set up. You will be asked for a code the next time you sign in.
done.totpSetUpNoCodes: Your authenticator app is set up. You will be asked for a code the next time you sign in. You hold no recovery codes — generate a set below, before you need it.
done.codesDiscarded: Those codes were thrown away and never stored. Whatever you had before is unchanged.
done.tlsRevoked: That TLS client certificate is revoked. A browser presenting it is refused from now on.
done.passkeyOne: Your passkey is ready. Create a second one on a different device or a security key, so that losing this one is not a locked account.
done.passkeyRemoved: That passkey is removed. If it was saved in a password manager, you can delete it there too.
done.riscStopping: You asked to stop sharing security events. It takes effect after the waiting period, and you can cancel until then.
done.riscShared: Security events about your account are shared.
done.codesSaved: Your {n} recovery codes are saved. Only their hashes are stored, so this service can never show them to you again — keep the copy you made.
done.keyOff: Your {rfc} signing key is off. Anything still signing with it will be refused from now on.
done.passkeyMany: Your passkey is ready. You hold {n} — if one is lost the others still sign you in.
